newsitem.title: USA: Lower borrowing costs to boost US housing - experts.
newsitem.headline: Lower borrowing costs to boost US housing - experts.

text.p: Lower borrowing costs are expected to have bolstered homebuilding activity in June, economists said.
June housing starts were expected to have risen to 1.45 million units from 1.397 million units, according to a Reuters poll of economists conducted on Friday.
Improved weather conditions likely propelled housing starts in the latest reporting month. Poor weather conditions -- rainfall -- dampened construction activity in May, economists noted.
"One primary reason for the expectations of higher housing starts is interest rates ... mortgage rates have dropped somewhat as a result," said Sung Won Sohn, an economist with Norwest Corp.
"We see more and more people coming back to the housing market," he said, noting that continued declines in interest rates were sure to bolster continued demand in the housing sector.

Michael Hoeh, vice president at Dreyfus Corp, agreed, noting that lower borrowing costs have already been acknowledged by other industry data such as the weekly Mortgage Bankers Association refinancing survey.

In the July 4 reporting week, Hoeh said, the MBA's seasonally adjusted purchase index component saw a 7.4-percent rise. That, he pointed out, "was a large increase for a one-week period" even in the summer season.
As a result, Hoeh said, this "generally points to a better economy and mortgage rates that are relatively low, which make homes more affordable to a typical potential buyer."
The expectations of a pick-up in housing starts may also be tied to heightened demand within the low to moderate-income housing market sector.
"There is a shortage of middle- to low-priced homes. They have been selling like hotcakes," said Norwest's Won Sohn, adding that builders catering to that sector likely will benefit.

Also, niche demand in the second-home market and homebuilding in economically booming communities such as California's Silicon Valley were expected to have underpinned June housing starts, said Richard Berner, chief economist at Mellon Bank.

Berner said he believed the recent drop in rates likely will be constructive for housing activity over the next few months. He had expected housing starts to falter in the second half of 1997, "but I'm starting to revise my thinking on that score."
One economist who expected June housing starts to rise does not, however, share as bright an assessment of the nation's housing sector.
Marilyn Schaja, an economist with Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp, said that an annualized level of 1.44 million may be the cap on activity.
"It (housing) won't pick up a lot given the rate decline," Schaja said.
The Commerce Department will release its June report on housing starts and permits on Thursday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
